content: Below are the detailed explanations of the key concepts: Mean: The mean is commonly referred to as the average. To calculate the mean, you sum up all the values in a dataset and divide by the total number of values. For example, if there are five individuals with the following number of televisions in their homes: 1, 4, 2, 0, and 3, the mean number of televisions is calculated as follows: [(1 + 4 + 2 + 0 + 3) / 5 = 2] Therefore, the mean number of televisions in this group is 2. 2. Median: The median represents the middle value in a dataset when the values are arranged in ascending or descending order. It is the point at which half of the data points lie above and half lie below. Using the same example of five individuals with 1, 4, 2, 0, and 3 televisions, when the data is ordered (0, 1, 2, 3, 4), the median is 2. This is because two individuals have fewer than 2 televisions, and two individuals have more than 2 televisions. Standard Deviation (SD): The standard deviation quantifies the amount of variation or dispersion in a dataset. Importantly, the standard deviation remains unaffected by the size of the sample. 2. Variance: Variance is the square of the standard deviation. 3. Standard Error of the Mean (SEM): The SEM quantifies how precisely the sample mean estimates the true population mean. It is always smaller than the standard deviation. As the sample size increases, the SEM decreases, indicating a more accurate estimate of the population mean. The SEM is mathematically related to the sample standard deviation (S) and the sample size. 4. 95% Confidence Interval: The 95% confidence interval provides a range within which the true population mean is expected to lie with 95% certainty. It is calculated as: [ text{Mean} pm 1.96 times text{Standard Error} ] 5. Coefficient of Variation (CV): The coefficient of variation is the ratio of the standard deviation ((sigma)) to the mean ((mu)). It is expressed as: [ c_{text{v}} = frac{sigma}{mu} ] A CV of less than 5% is generally considered acceptable in many fields, indicating low variability relative to the mean.
